In Carrow Ford, the news spread the way Osric wanted it to. By noon the whole town had heard that the toll-keeper's girl had wandered into the Reach after dark, that her poor mother had searched until dawn, and that nothing had been found but a scorched shoe. Osric told the story himself at the well, with his hat in his hands. He did not mention the charter. He did not need to. Everyone knew that with the child gone, the ford rights would pass to whoever held the toll-house, and that the Harvest Assize, where such claims were sealed, would sit on the bridge in three days.

Maren did not go to the well. She stayed in the toll-house with the shutters closed, and when the neighbours came with bread and sympathy, she did not open the door. Some of them said it was grief. It was not grief. It was the sound of the empty lantern hook by the gate, knocking against the wall every time the wind moved, and the knowledge that she had chosen, and that the choice could not be taken back.

Out in the Reach, Ailis and Tamsin waited for the river to fall. They lived on hard cheese and the fish Tamsin trapped in the shallows, and every evening Ailis lit the brass lantern and set it on the flat rock outside the hut. Every evening the grey one came, walked once around the light, and lay down beside it for the night. She never ate the fish. She never made a sound. But when Osric's men came riding along the valley rim on the second afternoon, searching for something they would not name out loud, the dragon rose from the ridge with her ash-grey scales catching the sun, and the riders turned their horses and did not come back. Tamsin said nothing about it, but from that night on she slept with her boots on.

On the third morning the river dropped. Tamsin woke Ailis before dawn, and they went down through the dead trees to the ford, where the water had pulled back to show a shelf of black mud and weed. Tamsin waded out to her knees and scraped at something with the end of her crook. Slowly a shape came out of the mud: a slab of grey stone, taller than a man, lying on its side where the flood had thrown it.

It was the charter stone, the one the ford-wardens had raised when the crossing was first made, long before there were toll-gates or tax-reeves or assizes. Carved into its face, blurred by water but still clear, was a spiral with three short lines running out from one side. And beside it, cut just as deep, was the outline of a folded wing, bent over the spiral as if to shelter it.

Ailis put her hand flat against the carving. Under her collar the whorl went warm again. Tamsin read the old letters aloud, slowly, tracing them with a wet finger. The crossing is kept by the marked, she read, and the marked are kept by the grey. Whoever bears the sign holds the ford, and no hand but theirs may seal it.

The ford-wardens had never been toll-keepers. They had been bonded to a dragon, and the dragon had kept the crossing safe for them, and the charter was not a tax right to be bought and sold. It was a promise, and the promise belonged to Ailis.

Tamsin pulled a roll of rough paper and a stick of charcoal from her oilskin, and together they took a rubbing of the whole stone, working fast, because the river was already rising. By the time they finished, the bells were ringing in Carrow Ford. The Assize had begun.
